submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires retrospectively on the concrete vocabulary of ordinary town-and-home life: the street and the public places a person passes, shops in or stays at (street, sidewalk, boulevard, alley, plaza, promenade, shop, store, bazaar, cafe, restaurant, bar, pub, hotel, motel, lounge, lobby, corridor), the shared rooms of a dwelling (home, room, kitchen, hall, porch, bathtub), and the small narrative words that put someone there (local, lived, sat, walked, went out, on his way, dinner, evening). It stays at zero on institutions and abstractions (library, museum, school, bank, church, hospital, market, square), on private rooms (bedroom, bathroom, garage, attic), on open landscape (river, forest, mountain, sea, field, farm) and on code, maths or other technical prose, even when a place word appears inside them.

Canada

Canada (/ ˈkænədə /; French: [ka.na.da]) is a country in the northern half of North America. Its ten provinces and three territories extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific and northward into the Arctic Ocean, covering 9.98 million square kilometres (3.85 million square miles), making it the world's second-largest country by total area and the fourth-largest country by land area. Canada's border with the United States is the world's longest land border. Canada is sparsely populated, the majority of its land territory being dominated by forest and tundra and the Rocky Mountains; about four-fifths of the country's population of 35 million people live near the southern border. The majority of Canada has a cold or severely cold winter climate, but southerly areas are warm in summer.

Canada has been inhabited for millennia by various Aboriginal peoples. Beginning in the 15th and 16th centuries, British and French claims were made on the area, with the colony of Canada first being established by the French in 1537. As a consequence of various conflicts, the United Kingdom gained and lost territories within British North America until it was left, in the late 18th century, with what mostly geographically comprises Canada today. Pursuant to the British North America Act, on July 1, 1867, the colonies of Canada, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia joined to form the semi-autonomous federal Dominion of Canada. This began an accretion of provinces and territories to the mostly self-governing Dominion to the present ten provinces and three territories forming modern Canada.

In 1931, Canada achieved near total independence from the United Kingdom with the Statute of Westminster 1931, and full sovereignty was attained when the Canada Act 1982 removed the last remaining ties of legal dependence on the Parliament of the United Kingdom. Canada is a federal parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, with Queen Elizabeth II being the head of state. The country is officially bilingual at the federal level. It is one of the world's most ethnically diverse and multicultural nations, the product of large-scale immigration from many other countries. Its advanced economy is the eleventh largest in the world, relying chiefly upon its abundant natural resources and well-developed international trade networks. Canada's long and complex relationship with the United States has had a significant impact on its economy and culture.

Canada is a developed country and has the tenth highest nominal per capita income globally as well as the ninth highest ranking in the Human Development Index. It ranks among the highest in international measurements of government transparency, civil liberties, quality of life, economic freedom, and education. Canada is a Commonwealth Realm member of the Commonwealth of Nations, a member of the Francophonie, and part of several major international and intergovernmental institutions or groupings including the United Nations, the North

Dun dun…dun dun…dun dun dun dun dun dun dun. Yep! You’ve all heard the famous theme song from Jaws, the movie that based on the hit Peter Benchley novel of the same name in the 1970s. It’s a classic movie (shame on you if you haven’t seen it) that bore famous lines such as “we’re going to need a bigger boat”. The story it tells is that of a small sea side town called Amity. A town that rarely experiences any form of crime. In fact, nothing ever happens. That is, except for the summertime when the beaches fill up as holidaymakers enjoy the sun sea and sand. That is, until a Great White Shark arrives, turning the lives of all that live there upside down.
The story paints a clear picture. A picture of a monster, a feeding machine that has blood lust for human flesh. It was at this point that sharks got widespread coverage as monsters of the deep. But there is a fundamental problem here. The fact is, sharks are extremely misunderstood. The picture portrayed by the book and by the movie was quite inaccurate. Indeed, the author Peter Benchley himself regretted the impact that his story had on sharks.
Sharks have been on Earth for around 400 million years. They have evolved to become the top predator in our oceans. Without them, our marine ecosystems would collapse. Sharks are amazing creatures but the often get overlooked because they aren’t as friendly as dolphins, whales or seals. These animals are seen as cute and fluffy. But who will stand up for the shark?
The movie “Jaws” is a simple movie, who’s concepts were fictional and depictions of shark behaviour – inaccurate, has now led to generation upon generation handing down a baseless fear of these amazing creatures.
“If I have one hope, it is that we will come to appreciate and protect these wonderful animals before we manage, through ignorance, stupidity and greed, to wipe them out altogether.”
– Peter Benchley (author of ‘Jaws’)
Shark populations face the threat of extinction in every part of the world primarily due to overfishing driven by the high demand for shark fins. However there are additional threats facing sharks that include by-catch, where sharks are killed when other seafood is being targeted, recreational fishing, sharks being used for ingredients in cosmetics or health supplements, destruction of habitat and more.
And did you know that shark fins are obtained by removing the fins of the shark while they are still alive before they are thrown back into the water leaving them helpless to other predators if they do not bleed out beforehand in absolute agony.
According to Oceana, of the nearly 500 species of sharks, only about a dozen are potentially dangerous to humans. Even for those species that are, humans aren’t preferred prey. Furthermore, they don’t attack people that often—certainly not enough to warrant their stereotype.
More needs to be done to protect these beautiful creatures from extinction. Educate yourself. Be wary of the products you purchase and what materials they are

Thumb joint pain is aggravating and very painful. The joint is located below the thumb and above the wrist and pain occurs when trying to pinch or grip and may continue even when at rest. Opening a jar with a twist lid or picking up a coin can cause waves of pain in the whole hand, fingers and wrist.
Thumb Joint Pain Common Causes
Consider how many times this joint is used. The thumb is used to pick up objects, to open doors and turn the pages of a book. It is used in typing and texting. No wonder the joint starts to break down after a while. Overuse causes the cushion between the two bones at the joint to wear down and once bone is rubbing against bone, pain and inflammation starts. Injury to the thumb also results in thumb joint pain. Severe sprains and jams to the thumb can start the problem. Arthritis may be the culprit as it causes a weakness in bones resulting in deterioration of the joint. Carpal Tunnel Syndrome is another cause of joint pain in the thumb. Typists use this joint continuously and this use causes nerves to compress in the wrist that extend to the thumb joint.
Thumb Joint Pain Symptoms
Pain is the most prevalent symptom. It radiates from the fingers to the wrist in severe cases, and is localized near the base of the thumb near the wrist in the fleshy palm of the hand. Pain sometimes is sharp in nature and occurs when turning a key, opening a door or any motion that causes the thumb to grip, pinch or rotate. Many times there is a loss of strength in the hand. The thumb may continue to ache even when resting or a bump may form over the joint to the point of affecting the appearance of the hand.
Several tests can reveal a problem with the thumb joint. An X-ray shows joint deterioration common with arthritis and also shows spurs or calcium deposits. Physical exams check for bumps or other deformities caused by the condition. The doctor may listen for grinding sounds while moving the thumb. Other tools that diagnose the problem are CT scans, MRI scans and bone scans.
Easy Home Treatments
Less severe thumb joint pain symptoms can be managed by applying alternating heat and cold. The heat eases pain and relaxes surrounding muscles. Application of cold also stops the pain. Put an ice pack on the joint for 15 minutes a few times a day or rub an ice cup over the palm area near the thumb for a few minutes. Follow with a heat pack or heating pad on the area for another 15 minutes. Some exercises may help mobility and pain. Hold the hand out with the palm up and lift the thumb as high as possible holding it up for five seconds. Hold the hand out with pinkie finger down and lift the thumb up holding it for five seconds. Hold the hand out with the palm forward and fingers up and rotate the thumb in circles in both directions. Start with five repetitions or rotations and work up to 20.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The train got in after dark. We left our bags at the hotel desk, crossed the lobby, and took a table at the bar, where the man behind it poured two glasses and told us the kitchen had closed half an hour before.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: a hotel lobby, bar and kitchen scene in a new context, dense with the claimed public-place and shared-room vocabulary, so the hypothesis predicts firing.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She put the kettle on in the kitchen, then went out onto the porch with her tea and watched the street until the lamps came on and the neighbours went in for dinner. Nobody passed the house after that except a dog.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: kitchen, porch, street, out and dinner in continuous narrative prose, testing the claimed vocabulary in a domestic frame unlike the top examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The tavern on the corner was full that night; men stood in the open door with their coats still on, and the smell of soup drifted down the pavement past the closed stalls to where the lamplighter was working.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout by paraphrase: a public place a person passes with none of the listed trigger tokens (tavern, pavement, stalls), so it tests whether the pole reads the town-and-home notion or only the enumerated words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They ate dinner at a little restaurant off the plaza, and afterwards walked the promenade with the evening crowd, past the shuttered shops and the fountain where the children were still playing long after the light had gone.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: dinner, restaurant, promenade and evening, plus walked and shops, in a new evening-town context that the hypothesis names as activating.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He took a motel room on the boulevard, sat in the dim lounge until the bar opened, then crossed the alley to the cafe and ordered breakfast from a woman who had been up since four.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: motel, room, lounge, bar, alley, cafe and sat all appear in a travel scene, a combination absent from the top examples but squarely inside the claimed vocabulary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They had lived in the same house for thirty years, and the long hall still smelled of the same polish; the front room was where he sat each evening with the paper, and nobody was allowed to move the chair.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: lived, hall, room, sat and evening in a dwelling, testing the claimed narrative words plus shared-room vocabulary in a wholly new sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: She scrubbed the bathtub, hung the towels on the line behind the house, and swept the front steps before the family came in for supper, because the visitors were expected at seven and there was no time in the morning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout: the word bathtub (whose final piece is the peak token of example 7) plus a domestic chore scene, testing the claimed dwelling vocabulary in ordinary home prose.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Day one: coffee at the cafe on the corner, then the covered bazaar where the spice stalls are. We stayed so long that we had dinner in a small restaurant behind the promenade, and the waiter brought out a plate of things we had not ordered.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Cross-genre holdout: a travel-guide voice rather than the pg19, c4 and fineweb-edu narratives, with cafe, dinner, restaurant and out as the activating vocabulary.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Nobody in the village could remember when the mill had stopped turning, and the road in from the valley had been widened twice since then. For most of the morning the only sounds were the water under the bridge and a dog barking somewhere above the trees. By noon, though, the main street had begun to fill: the baker propped his door open, the woman who sold flowers set out her buckets along the sidewalk, and the men who had finished at the yard drifted toward the cafe on the corner, where they stood with their hands in their pockets until the pub opened. Then they went in out of the wind, sat at the back, ordered dinner, and argued about the price of feed until the evening had gone.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout: the claimed town-and-home vocabulary (street, sidewalk, cafe, pub, sat, dinner, evening) sits deep in a passage over a hundred tokens long, testing the retrospective mechanism the hypothesis claims.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: After work I stopped at the store for milk, then took the long way home along the sidewalk where the cafes put their chairs out. The street was full of people and the evening was warm enough to sit outside with dinner.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Holdout in a modern first-person diary voice: store, way, home, sidewalk, street, evening and dinner, a register unlike the nineteenth-century examples.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The library closes at six on weekdays, and the upper floor is reserved for graduate students who have applied for a desk there; the rest of the building is open to anyone with a card, although the lifts stop at half past five.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: an institution the hypothesis explicitly puts at zero, written without any claimed place or narrative token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The school begins at eight, and the children are expected to line up in the yard before the first bell rings; visitors must report to the office on the ground floor and sign the book.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: school is on the hypothesis's zero list, and the yard and office here add no claimed dwelling or public-place token.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The hospital has added two wards since the flood, and the waiting lists for elective surgery are still longer than they were before the review; the new wing is not expected to open before the spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: hospital is named as an institution the pole stays at zero on, with no claimed vocabulary in the surrounding words.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The bank raised its prime rate by a quarter point, and analysts expect one more increase before the end of the year, when the board meets again to review the forecast and the budget.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: bank in its financial-institution sense, one of the hypothesis's declared zeros, in an abstract finance register.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The square was empty at that hour; the stalls had been taken down and only a few pigeons were left on the stones, and nobody crossed it until the first buses started running at dawn.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Hard negative: a town square, the most surprising item on the hypothesis's zero list given that it is physically a public place a person passes.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The market for used cars has softened, and dealers are cutting prices to clear inventory before the new models arrive in the autumn, when buyers usually come back in numbers.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The bathroom tap has been dripping for a week, and the landlord says the plumber will come on Friday with the parts he ordered in June, if he comes at all.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Two factors determine the load a beam can carry: the span between the supports and the stiffness of the section. In the tests reported here the span was held constant while the reinforcement was varied, and the deflection was measured at the midpoint after each load increment had been held for ten minutes. The readings were then corrected for temperature, because the laboratory is not climate controlled and the steel expands measurably over the course of a day. A least squares fit to the corrected data leaves a residual of 0.8 millimetres at the design load, well inside the tolerance given in the code. The same procedure was applied to a sample taken from the street outside the depot, and the results agreed with the values in the table.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context hard negative: a structural-engineering passage with the claimed street token once deep inside, testing the hypothesis's claim that technical prose stays at zero even when a place word appears in it.
